COLDWAR_IRQ_rcc_rules: The republic is governed through a Revolutionary Command Council, but the boundaries between president, party and army remain uncertain. We must establish whose orders carry the authority of the state before another struggle for office becomes a struggle for Iraq itself.
COLDWAR_IRQ_executive_state: Iraq cannot be rebuilt by committees that dispute every instruction from Baghdad. An appointed executive will give the government a clear direction, although those excluded from its councils will have little reason to regard its decisions as their own.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_compact: A state held together by the next arrest or promotion cannot command lasting confidence. We will seek a constitutional compact that gives competing interests a place in public life, accepting that a government answerable to more Iraqis must also spend longer reaching agreement.
COLDWAR_IRQ_provincial_agents: Orders issued in Baghdad often lose their force before reaching the districts. A stronger network of provincial officials will carry national policy into the countryside and improve revenue collection, but each new office adds another claim on the treasury.
COLDWAR_IRQ_elected_councils: Provincial government should hear more than the instructions of the capital. Local councils will give communities a voice in the services they receive, while Baghdad must provide the staff and funds needed to turn local representation into useful administration.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civil_register: A government cannot collect revenue or provide reliable services when its records are incomplete and unevenly maintained. A common civil register will give our ministries a firmer account of the people they serve and reduce dependence on personal introductions to local officials.
COLDWAR_IRQ_security_priority: The republic has too many enemies to leave its security services weak and divided. We will devote more trained officials and resources to protecting the government, even as that priority draws scarce expertise away from laboratories, schools and civilian ministries.
COLDWAR_IRQ_judicial_priority: A court whose judgment changes with the wishes of a minister offers little protection to anyone. We will strengthen judicial review and professional legal service, accepting limits on the executive in return for a state whose decisions carry greater public confidence.
COLDWAR_IRQ_review_detentions: Years of political conflict have filled prisons with cases that mix genuine violence, party rivalry and personal accusation. Reviewing individual detentions may help restore trust, but releasing opponents will also give them the freedom to organize against the government.
COLDWAR_IRQ_courts_budget: Legal guarantees mean little to an Iraqi who cannot reach a functioning court. Better staffing and provincial access will make justice less dependent on connections in Baghdad, although a professional bench requires salaries and facilities that cannot be supplied by decree.
COLDWAR_IRQ_ministerial_audit: Public employment has become entangled with personal loyalty and the distribution of favors. We will examine ministerial payrolls and redundant appointments, beginning the difficult work of making the administration serve its duties rather than the patrons who secured each post.
COLDWAR_IRQ_north_talks: The northern conflict cannot be settled by treating every Kurdish demand as a question of military obedience. We will open negotiations over regional authority and national belonging, knowing that Baghdad and the Kurdish leadership must both answer to constituencies suspicious of compromise.
COLDWAR_IRQ_army_command_review: An army cannot operate coherently when operational orders and procurement instructions arrive through competing channels. A review of command authority will clarify responsibilities, though the headquarters and inspections needed to enforce those boundaries will bring their own expense.
COLDWAR_IRQ_budget_accounts: The state budget should reveal what the government has promised and what it can afford. Clearer accounts will improve revenue administration and expose competing claims on public money, at the cost of discretion for ministers accustomed to arranging expenditure privately.
COLDWAR_IRQ_autonomy_guarantees: An autonomy agreement will survive only if its promises can be seen in schools, provincial offices and the distribution of funds. We must give the settlement practical substance, accepting the administrative burden of sharing authority rather than expecting a signature to end distrust.
COLDWAR_IRQ_professional_command: Personal access to senior officials must no longer substitute for an agreed military chain of command. By placing operations and professional responsibilities on a clearer footing, we can improve coordination and remove some of the uncertainty that has long weakened the army.
COLDWAR_IRQ_tax_registry: Oil revenue cannot excuse a tax administration that knows too little about the economy beneath it. Better registers and trained collectors will widen the state's financial reach, although building a dependable service requires more than sending another demand for payment.
COLDWAR_IRQ_state_compact: The republic now needs institutions that can carry political disagreement without falling apart. We will review the constitutional settlement and its obligations, seeking an order in which ministries, provinces and communities know both the authority they possess and the limits they must respect.
COLDWAR_IRQ_regional_command: The Baath governs Iraq, but a ruling party needs more than control of the principal offices. The Regional Command must coordinate its cadres and ministries if Arab unity, freedom and socialism are to become a coherent programme rather than competing claims to authority.
COLDWAR_IRQ_national_front: A wider front could draw organized workers and other political currents into the republic's programme. Cooperation will require room for partners to retain their own identity, placing limits on the Baath's freedom to govern as the sole voice of the nation.
COLDWAR_IRQ_baath_monopoly: Sharing the government invites rivals to build their influence under the shelter of our authority. We will reserve political leadership for the Baath and rely on its own cadres, gaining a clearer command while deepening the exclusion of those outside the party.
COLDWAR_IRQ_front_guarantees: A coalition cannot endure if its smaller parties are present only to applaud decisions already taken. A written charter will define their place in public life and government, requiring an apparatus capable of managing a partnership that will often disagree.
COLDWAR_IRQ_party_screening: A ministry hostile to the party can obstruct its programme without openly challenging the government. Appointments will face closer political scrutiny, even though excluding capable specialists for doubtful loyalty narrows the pool of people able to modernize the state.
COLDWAR_IRQ_baath_congress: The party's leadership must be settled within its own institutions rather than through whispered alliances among officeholders. A regional congress will give cadres a forum to weigh the direction of the Baath and the authority of those who speak in its name.
COLDWAR_IRQ_mass_party: The Baath should reach beyond a narrow circle of established organizers. Teachers, workers and provincial activists can carry its programme into everyday life, but a broader membership will demand an organization large enough to educate, coordinate and answer to them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_cadre_party: Numbers alone do not make a party capable of ruling. We will place our confidence in a disciplined core of trained cadres, strengthening internal direction while leaving many Iraqis to encounter the Baath as an authority above them rather than a movement they can join.
COLDWAR_IRQ_popular_organizations: Unions and professional associations can connect the republic to people rarely heard inside a ministry. Supporting these organizations will widen the party's social foundations, but their work needs resources and their members will expect more than instructions from the leadership.
COLDWAR_IRQ_party_schools: A growing party cannot depend entirely on personal loyalty to explain its purpose. Political schools will teach cadres a common language and programme, although the hours and teachers devoted to ideological instruction must come from an already limited supply of trained people.
COLDWAR_IRQ_baath_accounts: The resources of the party and those of the state cannot remain indistinguishable without damaging both. Separate accounts will make public obligations clearer, while denying party officials some of the informal freedom with which they have financed their political work.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_socialism: Political independence will remain incomplete if Iraq depends on others for its industrial future. Public enterprise will take a leading role in expanding production and employment, with the state accepting the continuing obligations that accompany a larger economic sector of its own.
COLDWAR_IRQ_secular_state: The republic needs competent officials from every religious community. We will make qualification and public duty the basis of state service, reducing the influence of confessional patronage while allowing a wider range of convictions inside the administration.
COLDWAR_IRQ_women_unions: Iraq cannot develop while much of its educated talent remains outside public employment. Greater access for women in teaching, medicine and administration will strengthen national expertise, but the institutions supporting that participation must receive sustained public backing.
COLDWAR_IRQ_enterprise_accounts: A public factory does not serve socialism merely because the state owns its gates. Managers must account for materials, costs and finished production so that national enterprise becomes a source of useful industrial capacity rather than a refuge from scrutiny.
COLDWAR_IRQ_baath_citizenship: The party claims to speak for a national republic, and its administration must meet that claim. Clear rules for access to public service will give citizenship a common meaning, even when equal treatment obstructs the preferences of influential local supporters.
COLDWAR_IRQ_party_social_bargain: The republic asks its citizens for loyalty and sacrifice; they will expect schools, care and a more secure life in return. The party must sustain the services on which its standing rests, accepting obligations that outlast any single political campaign.
COLDWAR_IRQ_baath_future: A party built to transform Iraq must also decide how it will govern beyond the ambitions of its present leaders. A cabinet committed to continuity can preserve the Baath's institutions and programme, though maintaining that machinery will remain a permanent public expense.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_presidency: Ahmad Hasan al-Bakr stands between the officer corps, the Baath leadership and a vice-president building his own authority. His presidency must reconcile these sources of power if the republic is to develop without another struggle among the men who claim to protect it.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_collective: No single office should be strong enough to swallow the institutions of the revolution. Al-Bakr will preserve a balance among senior leaders, gaining reassurance for the governing circle at the cost of slower decisions and more frequent negotiation.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_presidential: The president must be able to settle disputes that the party and military leadership cannot resolve among themselves. A stronger presidential apparatus will give al-Bakr the means to arbitrate, while concentrating more of the state's administration around his office.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_council: The Revolutionary Command Council should examine the choices made in its name. A greater role in budgets and appointments will restrain competing personal offices, although the president must accept that council scrutiny can also delay his own decisions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_loyal_officers: Al-Bakr knows the value of officers whose reliability has been tested in political uncertainty. Giving these men greater responsibility may strengthen military coordination, but experience in barracks does not replace the civilian expertise required by a modern administration.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_continuity: Officials should not have to rebuild the machinery of government whenever influence shifts inside the leadership. A permanent secretariat will preserve records and administrative knowledge, giving the presidency dependable information at the price of another institution to maintain.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_contain_deputy: The vice-president's growing reach risks turning delegated authority into an independent center of power. Al-Bakr will seek a clearer division of appointments and security responsibilities, though restraining an ambitious deputy requires concessions as well as presidential orders.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_delegate: Saddam has the energy and organizational ambition to drive work that the presidency cannot supervise alone. Wider delegation will give the executive a more forceful direction, while allowing the vice-president's influence to grow beyond the comfort of other senior figures.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_guarantees: Senior figures will not support an orderly transfer if they expect it to cost them every office and protection. Guarantees for the old guard can reduce the danger of a succession struggle, but preserving their place also preserves part of the patronage they command.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_deputy_budget: An executive cannot coordinate national development through personal instructions alone. The deputy's apparatus will receive the offices and staff needed to follow projects across ministries, making administration more active and also more expensive.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_development: Iraq's ambitions exceed the resources and skilled labor available to pursue them at once. Al-Bakr will establish clearer development priorities, directing national effort toward sustained construction while accepting that these commitments tie up more of the economy's resources.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_treaty: A closer relationship with the Soviet Union could support Iraq's development and international position. We will pursue a friendship treaty on negotiated terms, seeking useful cooperation without assuming that Moscow's commitments can be secured by Baghdad's wishes alone.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_north: A northern settlement will be judged by whether Baghdad honors its promises after the negotiations have ended. Al-Bakr must spend his own authority defending agreed guarantees against officials and supporters who would rather return to unrestricted central control.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_unity: The promise of Arab unity carries particular force when neighboring governments claim the same political tradition. Al-Bakr will explore cooperation with Syria, but a lasting union would require agreement between leaderships unwilling to become subordinate to one another.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_technical_mission: Foreign machinery is of limited value without Iraqis able to operate and maintain it. Technical missions will help train specialists, while deeper relationships with outside instructors and suppliers bring continuing expenses and dependencies of their own.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_compromise: The presidency has promised different institutions a place in the republic's future. Preserving those bargains requires patient administration and continued attention to their obligations; a compromise neglected once the immediate crisis passes will soon become another grievance.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_union_charter: Arab cooperation needs a clear account of where common authority begins and national authority ends. An agreed charter, or a more limited interstate council, can give partnership a durable form while requiring Iraq to moderate some of its independent diplomatic ambitions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_bakr_succession_plan: The republic should not discover the terms of succession only when the presidency falls vacant. Al-Bakr will seek an agreed transfer that protects institutional continuity, accepting that a negotiated departure leaves less room for the outgoing president to dictate every detail.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_presidency: Saddam Hussein intends to give the presidency an authority that competing institutions cannot easily dilute. His government promises decisive national direction, but consolidating that authority will unsettle those who hoped the republic would remain a balance among senior figures.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_personal_state: The president's decisions must carry through the entire executive without being weakened by rival patrons. A system centered on Saddam will tighten political direction, although the offices required to supervise loyalty and obedience will add to the machinery of government.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_party_cabinet: The Baath contains officials whose experience cannot be replaced by presidential confidence alone. A cabinet with room for ministerial argument can keep these interests invested in the government, provided the president accepts some restraint on the speed and reach of his own instructions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_security_bureau: A presidency determined to control its rivals needs a security apparatus that can reach beyond the capital's formal institutions. Expanding that apparatus will reinforce political discipline, but surveillance and coercion demand money and deepen the mistrust between the state and its citizens.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_technocrats: Industrial ambition depends on engineers and administrators whose usefulness is greater than their political connections. Protecting competent managers will help our enterprises improve, even when their professional judgment conflicts with demands for another convenient party appointment.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_social_contract: Oil wealth offers the presidency a powerful claim to legitimacy: a stronger state should bring a better daily life. Services and public provision can broaden support for Saddam's government, but they also create expectations that must be financed long after their announcement.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_guard: The president requires formations whose first loyalty is to the survival of his government. A strengthened guard will provide a dependable military core, while its preferred access to trained men and resources places a heavier burden on the defense budget.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_regular_army: National strength cannot rest entirely on a favored formation close to the presidency. Investing in the regular army's professional institutions will improve its coherence, though a force trained to common standards takes longer to prepare than one assembled around immediate political need.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_guard_supply: A guard expected to act rapidly cannot depend on uncertain access to depots and transport. Its own supply organization will improve readiness, while the personnel and administration of a separate logistical service make presidential protection a continuing expense.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_staff_college: Military appointments should reflect an officer's ability to direct and sustain operations. Staff training will give the army a stronger professional foundation, but respecting that foundation means accepting that political preference cannot settle every promotion and command.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_regional_role: Iraq has the resources and ambitions to demand a greater voice in regional affairs. A more active diplomatic establishment will advance that claim, although influence requires sustained work abroad and a larger apparatus to support Baghdad's commitments.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_iran_dossier: Revolution across the frontier has changed the assumptions on which Iraq has dealt with Iran. The presidency must assess the new leadership, unresolved disputes and the dangers of confrontation before choosing how far to press Iraq's position.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_industry: Presidential ambition must leave more behind than speeches and portraits. Expanding civilian industry will strengthen the productive base on which our wider programme depends and give the government a tangible answer to those waiting for development to reach them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_credit: The Gulf's governments have an interest in Iraq's strength, but that does not make their resources ours to command. We will seek credit through negotiation, accepting that money obtained for today's needs becomes a claim on the revenues of tomorrow.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_bounded_deterrence: A credible deterrent begins with troops able to hold their positions and commanders able to sustain them. Greater readiness will make threats against Iraq more costly, while retaining trained personnel and maintaining that readiness will place lasting demands on the treasury.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_local_procurement: An army dependent on foreign deliveries remains vulnerable even when its stores appear full. Strengthening local procurement and maintenance will help Iraqi industry support national needs and make better use of the machinery and expertise already available.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_debt_service: Credit that once appeared to demonstrate Arab solidarity now carries demands for repayment. The presidency must decide how much revenue it can devote to creditors without abandoning the domestic commitments on which its authority and prestige depend.
COLDWAR_IRQ_saddam_legacy: Saddam's presidency seeks to identify the strength of the republic with the strength of its leader. Turning that ambition into a durable political order will require continued attention to security, public consent and the expensive institutions built around presidential authority.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_council: The return of military government promises discipline after years of party conflict. An officer council around Abd al-Rahman Arif can draw on the authority of the army, but Iraqis who remember successive interventions will question whether this one offers a lasting political answer.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_caretaker: The army can claim to protect the republic without claiming the right to govern it forever. A caretaker administration will prepare a return to civilian authority, reassuring those outside the barracks while restricting the freedom of officers to rule by immediate command.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_permanent: Civilian rivalry has repeatedly drawn the military into the affairs of state. We will recognize the officer corps as the enduring foundation of the presidency, accepting that permanent military rule requires a permanent administrative presence beyond the barracks.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_civilian_cabinet: Officers cannot supervise every road, public enterprise and ministry with equal competence. A civilian cabinet of specialists will direct reconstruction, provided the military leadership is willing to leave some decisions to people whose authority comes from expertise rather than rank.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_garrisons: The army's presence offers the government a reach that many civilian offices still lack. Garrison commands will take a larger role in local administration and revenue collection, extending military responsibilities and the payroll needed to carry them out.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_procurement: Inflated contracts and neglected maintenance consume resources that the armed forces can ill afford to waste. Closer scrutiny of procurement will improve the work of our suppliers, though effective inspection requires an administrative service with the independence and means to examine them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_merit: An officer should advance because he can command, rather than because he knows which door to approach in Baghdad. Professional promotion will strengthen the army, while weakening the personal assurances through which the government has held its senior supporters together.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_loyalty: A commander who turns his troops against the government is more dangerous than any political pamphlet. Promotions will favor men whose loyalty is beyond doubt, even where that preference places reliable allies ahead of more capable military professionals.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_staff: The next generation of Iraqi officers needs a common grounding in staff work and operational discipline. A national college will strengthen the army's ability to recover and coordinate, although thorough professional preparation cannot be rushed to satisfy an immediate demand for formations.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_commissars: The military government needs trusted representatives inside the ministries charged with carrying out its programme. Appointing officers to these posts will tighten executive direction, while adding another layer of supervision to an administration already short of clear responsibilities.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_state_budget: Defense must be treated as an obligation of the state rather than an account beyond civilian comprehension. Bringing its expenditure into clearer public accounts will improve financial discipline, at the cost of discretion for commanders accustomed to arranging their own priorities.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_amnesty: The republic cannot keep every former opponent permanently outside public life. A conditional amnesty may draw some back into lawful politics, but the government must negotiate the terms carefully if reconciliation is to survive the suspicions of both soldiers and civilians.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_border_force: Frontier defense needs forces prepared for the ground they are expected to hold. Dedicated border formations will strengthen local readiness without placing the entire country on a permanent war footing, although their training and personnel must remain funded in peacetime.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_civic_timetable: A promise to relinquish power becomes less convincing each time its date is postponed. We will begin negotiating a public transition timetable, giving civilian politics a defined route forward while asking the officer corps to accept an end to its direct rule.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_reintegration: Units drawn into government duties must be able to return to military service without becoming a resentful political reserve. Clear assignments and an orderly withdrawal from civilian offices will help restore the distinction between commanding soldiers and governing citizens.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_logistics: Separate commands should not compete for transport and supplies that belong to the same armed forces. A unified logistical service will reduce waste, provided the government supports the professional headquarters and record keeping needed to direct it.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_continuity: Officers will be more willing to leave government if the terms of their future service are clear. Civilian guarantees can protect the army's legitimate defense responsibilities, while binding the new authorities to the personnel obligations accepted during the transition.
COLDWAR_IRQ_officer_settlement: Whether the army retains the presidency or returns to the barracks, Iraq needs a defined relationship between military command and political authority. An agreed civil-military order will make service more coherent while limiting the discretion of those at the top.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_republican_movement: Iraq's Arab republican currents still offer an alternative to Baathist leadership, but they must rebuild a common political purpose. A renewed movement can gather these supporters around social reform and Arab solidarity, while reopening disputes over who has the right to lead them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_cairo: Cairo remains an important center of Arab political life, whatever course its government now follows. Closer cooperation may strengthen our wider relationships, although a partnership with a more influential Arab capital will also constrain Baghdad's freedom to set the regional agenda alone.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_iraqi_sovereignty: Arab solidarity should strengthen Iraq rather than leave its cabinet waiting for instructions from elsewhere. We will build an Arab republic rooted in Iraqi political consent, accepting a less commanding regional posture in order to preserve control over national decisions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_joint_planning: Shared political language is a poor substitute for practical cooperation. Joint civilian planning can turn Arab partnership toward development and useful exchange, but each government must agree to its obligations before grand declarations can become work on the ground.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_public_service: A republican state should recruit officials for their ability to serve rather than their proximity to a political patron. Competitive recruitment will make administration more efficient, even when it denies movement leaders appointments they regard as rewards for loyalty.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_social_charter: The promise of Arab socialism must reach the worker and farmer as more than a public slogan. A social charter will commit the republic to services and reform, giving our programme a clearer purpose and the treasury a continuing responsibility.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_state_sector: Private interests alone cannot be expected to build the industrial foundations of national independence. Public enterprise will lead development, concentrating resources on sustained production while committing a larger share of the economy to the state's economic responsibilities.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_mixed_sector: A national economy has room for both public ambition and private initiative. Allowing independent suppliers a greater role can make production more adaptable, though the government must accept a smaller direct claim on the income generated beyond its own enterprises.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_state_contracts: Public investment needs suppliers able to deliver useful production rather than cultivate the right political introduction. More accountable contracting will strengthen our industrial programme, provided inspectors and administrators have the resources to follow work beyond the signing of an agreement.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_credit_coops: Small producers cannot modernize their holdings on patriotic appeals alone. Cooperative credit will help them obtain the means to improve production, while the republic accepts the continuing support needed to make rural lending serve more than the best-connected borrowers.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_citizenship: Arab identity cannot excuse unequal treatment of the people who share Iraq's citizenship. A common civic standard will broaden confidence in the republic, even where it restrains officials who would prefer to distribute access and recognition according to their own political loyalties.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_palestine: Solidarity with the Palestinians is an important measure of our Arab commitments. Better organized assistance can make Iraqi support more useful, but effective cooperation requires sustained administration and an understanding with those who are meant to receive it.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_technical_exchange: Arab cooperation should help train the people who will build and administer the republic. Technical exchanges will widen the experience of our specialists, while the offices needed to arrange placements and follow their work must be maintained at home.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_union_convention: A lasting Arab union cannot be assembled by announcing that existing disagreements have disappeared. A convention will let the participating governments define common powers and reserved rights, giving unity a chance to rest on consent rather than the ambitions of one capital.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_civil_diplomacy: Civilian assistance can build relationships that outlast a diplomatic speech. Iraq will work with its partners on support they are prepared to accept, gaining influence through cooperation while leaving ministers less freedom to announce commitments without consulting those involved.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_training_network: A durable partnership needs specialists who can work across national institutions. A wider training network will strengthen practical knowledge, although exchanges, instructors and places of study require continuing support rather than occasional gestures of friendship.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_union_accounts: The costs of Arab partnership must be as clear as its political aspirations. Agreed accounts will help participating governments meet their commitments and organize revenue, while the administration of common work adds responsibilities that each partner must be prepared to sustain.
COLDWAR_IRQ_arab_republic_endures: The future of Iraq cannot wait indefinitely for agreement on the future of every Arab state. Our republic will pursue its social and national programme at home, preserving the ambition of wider solidarity without making domestic government dependent on a successful union.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_congress: The Iraqi Communist Party carries the wounds of repression and bitter internal division. A congress must restore a common organization and purpose, giving surviving cadres a way to rebuild political work without pretending that the losses of earlier struggles have been undone.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_front_strategy: Cooperation with the Baath may secure space for workers' organization and social reform. Such a front must remain conditional, since a place in government will be worth little if the Communist Party loses the freedom to speak and organize for itself.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_independent_strategy: The party cannot build a socialist future by depending on the tolerance of stronger rivals. An independent course will preserve its political initiative, but it also leaves communists more exposed to confrontation with forces unwilling to accept their claim to national leadership.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_legal_cells: Legal recognition gives the party an opportunity to replace secrecy with open organization. Offices and local networks can bring communists closer to the communities they seek to represent, provided the guarantees that allow them to work are honored and defended.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_underground: The experience of repression warns against leaving every cadre and contact exposed. Maintaining an underground organization will protect continuity when political conditions worsen, although secrecy imposes costly duplication and makes open, accountable political work more difficult.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_membership: Scattered branches need to know who can still organize, teach and maintain contact with supporters. Restoring membership records will reconnect the party's surviving strength, giving its leadership a more dependable foundation than optimistic claims about support it cannot yet reach.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_democratic_front: Socialism need not require every public organization to become an extension of the party. A pluralist front can draw wider confidence and political participation, provided communists accept that legal allies and opponents will continue to argue against their preferred course.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_vanguard: A revolutionary government cannot allow its programme to be undone by competing centers of political authority. The party will establish itself as the directing force of the state, strengthening discipline while alienating Iraqis unwilling to exchange one political monopoly for another.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_union_autonomy: Workers need organizations able to bargain with the government as well as support it. Independent unions will give that principle substance, though negotiated wages, workplace demands and industrial disagreement will impose costs that a socialist cabinet cannot simply dismiss.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_state_unions: Production and labor policy should be coordinated through the national plan. Integrating union bargaining into that system will help public industry pursue common targets, while risking resentment among workers who expect their representatives to challenge management rather than explain its decisions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_national_question: A socialist republic must address the Kurdish question without assuming that class solidarity has erased national demands. A nationalities charter will recognize the need for agreed rights and representation, giving the state responsibilities that require continuing attention beyond party declarations.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_industrial_workers: Workers' councils should understand the workshops whose future they debate. Practical workplace administration will connect representation to production, requiring trained delegates and clear records rather than leaving industrial management to competing slogans from the shop floor and the ministry.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_soviet_relations: Relations with Soviet communists can offer experience and practical cooperation, but Iraq's circumstances remain its own. We will seek an agreement that strengthens our work without treating friendship between parties as a substitute for negotiating the responsibilities of their governments.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_rural_cells: Land reform cannot be defended solely from offices in Baghdad. Rural organizers will help poorer farmers obtain advice and carry their demands to the government, while a lasting presence in scattered communities requires staff, transport and sustained local work.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_safety_inspection: Workers should not be asked to accept dangerous conditions merely because an enterprise belongs to the people. A stronger inspection service will make that principle credible, although safer procedures and proper oversight will sometimes slow production and add administrative expense.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_cadre_schools: The party needs cadres who can administer an enterprise or a school as well as explain its political line. Technical education alongside political instruction will strengthen that competence, provided training receives the staff and support it requires.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_peasant_credit: Rural producers need access to credit on terms that do not return them to dependence on powerful intermediaries. Reforming cooperative lending will support agricultural work, while requiring the government to accept a smaller immediate return from the people it is helping.
COLDWAR_IRQ_icp_socialist_republic: A socialist constitution should define how power is exercised and how the rights it proclaims can be defended. We will give the chosen political settlement a durable form, accepting that binding guarantees also limit the discretion of the party that sponsors them.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_secretariat: Aziz Muhammad must lead a party whose survival has depended on both discipline and accommodation. His secretariat will bring direction to its competing tasks, while rebuilding the organization needed to connect national leadership with cadres working under very different local conditions.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_negotiated_road: Aziz Muhammad can seek a place for communists within a broader governing arrangement without surrendering the party's separate identity. This road offers room to work, but the negotiations and compromises it demands will restrict the leadership's freedom to act alone.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_opposition_road: A subordinate place beside stronger parties may leave communists sharing responsibility without possessing real authority. Aziz Muhammad will build an independent opposition bloc, preserving its convictions while accepting the tension that a more openly confrontational course brings to national politics.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_front_red_lines: Cooperation must have limits that party members can recognize and defend. Clear guarantees for communist organization will give Aziz Muhammad a firmer basis for negotiation, although insisting on those guarantees may require him to refuse arrangements that promise easier immediate access to power.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_resilient_networks: The party has learned how quickly public organization can be broken when protection disappears. Better communications and dependable local contacts will help preserve its continuity, at the expense of maintaining a network whose work is often necessarily slow and discreet.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_congress_accounts: The general secretary's authority must remain answerable to the party he leads. Giving congress a meaningful review of the leadership will widen confidence in its decisions, while requiring Aziz Muhammad to win agreement where he might otherwise issue an instruction.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_federal_guarantees: Kurdish rights cannot depend on the goodwill of whichever minister next controls Baghdad. A federal settlement must provide authority that can be exercised and defended, committing the state to the offices and continuing work needed to make shared government credible.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_unitary_left: A single national budget can direct resources toward a common development programme. Aziz Muhammad will retain that central authority while offering local rights, but Kurdish partners and other regional interests may regard promises without a stronger constitutional position as insufficient.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_regional_budget: The terms of a federal compact must be visible in the services a region can provide. Education and local administration need dependable funding if autonomy is to become an ordinary part of government rather than a recurring argument over unfulfilled promises.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_language_rights: A child should not have to leave a language behind to obtain an education. Bilingual materials and trained teachers will give cultural rights practical meaning, while asking the central education service to support a more demanding and varied system of schooling.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_soviet_distance: Friendship with the Soviet Union need not require agreement on every question facing Iraq. Aziz Muhammad will preserve cooperative relations while asserting the party's own judgment, accepting that a less assertive regional posture may accompany that diplomatic room to disagree.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_worker_training: Industrial workers need opportunities to acquire the skills that a modern economy demands. Technical training will help public production improve through knowledge rather than exhortation, with the government accepting education as a continuing responsibility toward the workforce.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_united_opposition: Opponents of repression do not share a single view of Iraq's political or religious future. A minimum democratic charter can provide common ground, allowing Aziz Muhammad to seek cooperation without demanding that every prospective partner first become a communist.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_civilian_welfare: Regional prestige must not consume the resources needed for a decent civilian life. Aziz Muhammad will place welfare ahead of the military establishment's preferred spending, asking the republic to sustain social commitments even when its neighbors measure strength through arms.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_workplace_delegates: Workers' participation should give those on the shop floor a continuing voice in how an enterprise operates. Delegates can improve cooperation and planning, although consultation takes time and some demands will interrupt the uninterrupted production sought by managers.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_safe_return: Repression has driven capable Iraqis away from the institutions that need them. An orderly return, supported by legal review and administrative assistance, can recover some of that experience while confronting the unresolved cases and suspicions that exile leaves behind.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_rural_services: The countryside cannot remain an occasional destination for officials announcing another reform. Schools, clinics and practical assistance must become dependable local services, helping rural communities improve their livelihoods while creating obligations the state must support year after year.
COLDWAR_IRQ_aziz_party_renewal: A party claiming to represent working people must be able to reconsider the mandate of its own leadership. A renewal vote will let members judge Aziz Muhammad's course and the alternatives before them, making continuity something to be earned rather than assumed.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_reconstitution: Civilian politics in Iraq has been weakened by bans, military intervention and the dominance of armed organizations. Rebuilding its older traditions will require patient cooperation among those who favor representative government but disagree over the social and economic republic it should serve.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_social_republic: Political rights offer little reassurance to families without dependable public services. A social republic will place provision alongside representation at the center of its programme, while accepting that social commitments must be maintained by an equally durable public budget.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_liberal_republic: Independent enterprise should have room to invest without seeking permission from every political office. A liberal republic will encourage that initiative, accepting that an economy with more freedom outside the state also gives the treasury a less direct claim on its proceeds.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_social_budget: The social rights promised by our constitution will be judged in classrooms and public institutions. Sustained funding will give those promises substance, requiring ministers to defend continuing expenditure even when other interests call for a less demanding interpretation of the republic's obligations.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_commercial_courts: A contract that depends on political favor is a poor foundation for investment. Professional commercial courts will give economic activity a more predictable setting, while a legal service capable of resolving disputes properly requires judges, trained staff and regular public support.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_electoral_register: A credible election begins before the first ballot is cast. Reliable registers and a functioning electoral administration will let citizens contest their government through lawful politics, replacing vague promises of representation with the painstaking work needed to recognize and count voters.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_federal: A representative republic should give its regions a defined place in the constitutional order. Federal authority can make the union more acceptable to its different communities, although shared government requires institutions able to manage disagreements and responsibilities at more than one level.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_unitary: Equal citizenship can be served through a common treasury and national institutions. We will retain a unitary republic with elected local services, accepting the political restraint needed to let those institutions answer to their communities rather than every preference of the cabinet.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_fiscal_federalism: Regions cannot exercise meaningful responsibilities while depending on uncertain transfers from Baghdad. A revenue-sharing settlement will give federal government a practical basis, while limiting the share of national income that the central cabinet can direct entirely according to its own priorities.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_local_accounts: Local representation must be accompanied by accounts that residents and national authorities can examine. Better municipal records will strengthen revenue administration and service delivery, with a continuing inspection service needed to make accountability more than an entry in the constitution.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_security_oversight: Security services should defend the republic under rules that its citizens can understand. Civilian oversight will bring greater confidence in their work, while limiting the emergency powers and political discretion through which earlier governments sought to protect themselves.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_education: Citizens cannot participate fully in public life when schooling remains beyond their reach. The republic will support teacher training and wider access to education, giving its constitutional promises a stronger foundation among communities long distant from Baghdad's political debates.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_non_alignment: Iraq should be able to work with foreign governments without placing its diplomacy beyond public judgment. Cabinet and parliamentary review will give external partnerships a firmer domestic basis, though the need to defend each commitment will reduce freedom for private diplomatic bargains.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_labour_bargain: A civilian republic needs a settlement between the people who work in industry and those who direct it. Bargaining over wages and conditions can build consent, but the government must accept that a negotiated workplace will not always deliver production at the lowest immediate cost.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_universities: Universities need room to pursue knowledge and question the assumptions of those in power. Public support and academic autonomy will strengthen Iraqi scholarship, while allowing criticism to emerge from institutions that ministers might prefer to treat as another arm of government.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_credit_terms: Foreign credit creates obligations that extend beyond the cabinet which accepts it. Parliamentary scrutiny will make the terms of borrowing open to debate, allowing Iraq to seek finance while requiring its ministers to defend the commitments they propose to the country.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_union_compact: Workplace rights need mediators and inspectors able to resolve disputes before they become a test of political strength. A funded labor compact will make industrial relations more predictable, provided both government and employers accept the authority and expense of that service.
COLDWAR_IRQ_civic_mandate: A civilian government proves its authority by accepting that citizens may choose a different one. We will review the cabinet's programme and prepare the ground for another contestable mandate, placing constitutional continuity above the convenience of those currently in office.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_charter: A restored crown cannot govern as though the upheavals of the republic never occurred. A new charter must define the monarchy's place in today's Iraq, grounding its claim to continuity in an agreement that also recognizes how much the country has changed.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_ceremonial: The crown can stand above political rivalry only if it allows elected ministers to govern. A ceremonial monarchy will offer a symbol of continuity, while requiring the sovereign to accept that policy and parliamentary support belong to the cabinet rather than the palace.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_executive: A sovereign expected to preserve national unity should possess the authority to act when politicians fail. A stronger royal executive will give the palace a more direct role, but those who sought representative government will question the limits of its intervention.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_parliament: A parliament worthy of the new charter must be able to hold ministers responsible. Supporting a genuine contest for government will strengthen the settlement, although representative institutions require staff and administration as well as the willingness of the palace to accept disagreement.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_council: The crown needs advice that reaches beyond the personal access of a few favored figures. A permanent advisory council will give royal government a broader administrative foundation, while creating an institution whose offices and expectations must be supported by the state.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_accounts: The royal household and the national treasury must have clear and separate obligations. Open accounts will strengthen public finance and confidence in the crown, while limiting the informal discretion through which palace interests might otherwise draw upon state resources.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_land_review: Restoration will raise difficult claims over property and the land reforms of the republican years. The monarchy must examine these disputes without promising a wholesale return to the old order, accepting the administrative work needed to prevent its return from becoming a rural crisis.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_property_guarantees: Investment needs confidence that today's holdings will not be overturned by every change of government. We will protect existing property while leaving compensation claims for legal examination, though both former owners and present occupants may consider that balance insufficient.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_compensation: Disputed property cannot be settled fairly through a general promise to either restore or reject every claim. A tribunal will examine cases individually, seeking a settlement that respects current rural livelihoods while acknowledging that unresolved losses continue to carry political weight.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_rural_contracts: Farmers need enforceable agreements as much as merchants in the capital do. Better rural access to contract law will help agricultural production rest on clearer terms, provided the courts and officials needed to serve scattered communities receive sustained support.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_citizenship: The crown must belong to all citizens rather than one community or circle of families. Common constitutional rights will broaden confidence in the restored monarchy, even when equal treatment restrains the expectations of supporters who helped bring it back.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_jordan: A shared Hashemite connection offers a basis for renewed talks with Jordan. Cooperation may bring the two kingdoms closer, but any lasting arrangement must answer the interests of both governments rather than presume that dynastic ties have already settled their political differences.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_service: A modern monarchy needs officials who owe their position to public competence rather than royal favor. Professional recruitment will make government more efficient, at the price of denying the palace some of the appointments through which it could otherwise reward supporters.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_education: The restored monarchy must speak to a generation whose expectations have been formed by the republic. Civic and technical education will prepare more Iraqis to participate in national life, giving the constitutional settlement a foundation beyond loyalty to the royal family.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_commerce: The crown can use its diplomatic standing to seek commercial relationships useful to Iraq. A partnership must still be negotiated on practical terms, since friendship and ceremony alone cannot supply the investment or commitments our development requires.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_public_works: Public works should be understood as a duty of government rather than a gift from the sovereign. More coherent direction will help construction proceed, while the civil administration must be equipped to follow projects beyond their ceremonial opening.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_budget_review: Representatives must be able to examine what the state spends in the name of crown and country. A regular budget review will improve financial discipline, while requiring ministers and the palace to justify obligations they might otherwise prefer to arrange privately.
COLDWAR_IRQ_royal_settlement: The monarchy's future rests on a clear understanding between sovereign, cabinet and representatives. A settled constitutional charter will give each a recognized place, accepting that lasting confidence requires limits which remain binding even when the palace finds them inconvenient.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_national_government: A KDP-led cabinet must govern a country larger and more varied than the movement's northern strongholds. It will need institutions capable of translating Kurdish political experience into national administration, while reassuring Iraqis who fear that a new government will serve only one region.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_autonomy: The demand for autonomy is a demand for authority that can be exercised, not another promise dependent on Baghdad's goodwill. A workable accord will define regional responsibilities within Iraq, with institutions strong enough to give the agreement daily meaning.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_federal_republic: Federalism offers a way to place Kurdish rights within a wider Iraqi constitutional settlement. Such a republic must win confidence beyond the north, and its distribution of authority will necessarily leave the central government with less freedom to command national resources alone.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_autonomy_budget: Regional authority cannot survive on an empty account. Schools and public services must have dependable support if autonomy is to improve ordinary life, creating continuing obligations that both Kurdish leaders and the national government must be prepared to honor.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_federal_budget: A federal settlement needs agreement on how national revenue reaches the institutions responsible for local services. Negotiating that distribution will help make shared government credible, while requiring an administration capable of reconciling claims that will not always agree.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_government_accounts: Kurdish and Iraqi public accounts must be clear enough for their governments to work together. Better records will strengthen revenue administration and reveal overlapping obligations, though reliable financial cooperation requires staff and scrutiny beyond the immediate circle of party leadership.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_barzani_continuity: The movement's established networks have carried it through conflict and political uncertainty. Continuing to rely on the Barzani leadership will preserve organizational discipline, while maintaining the relationships and obligations that bind this traditional source of authority together.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_civic_party: The KDP must be able to represent people through public institutions as well as established personal loyalties. A more professional civic organization can widen its standing, although its leaders must accept limits on the inherited authority that has long helped hold the movement together.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_succession: The movement's future cannot be left to competing assumptions about who should inherit its leadership. A council will give the KDP a place to settle continuity and renewal, asking its leading figures to reach an agreement that their supporters can recognize.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_civic_councils: Local government should answer to the communities it serves as well as the party that helped establish it. Regional councils will broaden public participation, while requiring the staff and regular administration needed to make accountability possible outside the movement's own structures.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_language: Kurdish-language schooling and public service must be available in practice if cultural rights are to be trusted. Teachers, materials and trained officials will give those rights a daily presence, with continuing support needed to maintain services across the region.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_mountain_routes: Mountain communities remain difficult to reach, leaving farmers and local officials dependent on slow and uncertain journeys. Improving roads around Erbil will draw these districts closer to markets and services and give regional administration a firmer physical connection to the people it serves.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_oil_status: Kirkuk joins questions of oil, mixed communities and disputed political authority in a single difficult settlement. Its future must be negotiated rather than assumed, with guarantees that recognize why control of the city matters so deeply to more than one side.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_security_integration: Regional fighters and national forces need agreed duties if political compromise is to survive the next security crisis. Integration will require clear command arrangements and dependable pay, making military cooperation an obligation that the government must finance as well as proclaim.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_rural_credit: Mountain farming needs practical support adapted to communities distant from the main centers of investment. Credit and agricultural advice will help rural producers improve their work, while regional authorities accept the continuing costs of reaching places where ordinary lending is scarce.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_shared_revenue: Oil revenue must support the settlement that allows Iraq's communities to govern together. An accepted formula will make financial responsibilities clearer and strengthen public accounts, but maintaining confidence will require regular administration and adherence to the terms on both sides.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_local_policing: Police trusted by local communities can make civilian order less dependent on military confrontation. A regional charter will set professional duties and responsibilities, with training and administration needed to ensure that local authority serves the public rather than another private network.
COLDWAR_IRQ_kdp_common_republic: The chosen settlement must become an ordinary framework of government rather than a truce awaiting the next dispute. A common republic will require leaders in Baghdad and the regions to respect obligations that bind their own hands as well as protect their rights.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_government: Jalal Talabani's movement offers a different Kurdish political leadership, but a national government must answer questions that regional opposition can leave unresolved. Building a governing apparatus will give its programme direction while adding responsibilities that political organization alone cannot carry.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_pluralist_left: A progressive movement can draw strength from more than one political tradition. A broad Kurdish left will allow disagreement within a common programme, widening its appeal while requiring the leadership to persuade partners whose support cannot simply be commanded.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_disciplined_party: A movement divided over every decision may struggle to defend any common course. Tighter party discipline will give the leadership a more dependable organization, but supporters attracted by a broader political promise may resent the narrowing of space for dissent.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_local_assemblies: Representative assemblies need more than a hall in which to meet. Staff and regular budgets will let provincial institutions examine local needs and hold officials to account, turning political participation into useful administration at a continuing public cost.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_cadre_training: A progressive programme needs organizers who understand accounts, public enterprise and the work of local government. Technical training will make cadres more useful in office, provided the party supports practical competence alongside the political convictions that first brought them together.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_federal_platform: Kurdish political demands need a place in a national programme that other Iraqis can understand and debate. A federal platform will set out how shared government might work, requiring institutions capable of turning a regional aspiration into a countrywide constitutional settlement.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_regional_cooperation: Rival Kurdish movements have reasons to compete, but their supporters also depend on services that political division can weaken. We will seek cooperation with the KDP on common regional institutions, accepting negotiation where party independence might otherwise invite a separate course.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_independent_movement: Cooperation must not leave the PUK unable to advance the programme that distinguishes it from its rivals. A separate organization will preserve political initiative, while the additional offices and relationships needed to work independently will make regional administration more costly.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_joint_services: Shared institutions will be judged by whether they can provide dependable services across party boundaries. Supporting agreed regional administration can give cooperation a visible purpose, though common work requires continuing resources as well as willingness to share responsibility.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_party_municipalities: Local service networks can give the movement a durable connection to the communities it represents. Better municipal administration will strengthen revenue collection, while building a distinct apparatus commits the party to offices and responsibilities that must be sustained beyond campaigning.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_constitution: Federal Iraq needs national rules negotiated by those expected to live under them. A convention will give regional and national representatives a place to debate authority, rights and responsibilities, rather than leaving the country's future to separate promises made by rival leaderships.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_sulaymaniyah: Sulaymaniyah needs productive opportunities capable of supporting more than the immediate demands of political organization. A larger civilian industrial base will give the city a stronger place in regional development and help connect the movement's social ambitions to useful economic work.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_universities: Regional universities can train specialists while bringing students into contact with ideas beyond their own district. A network open to Iraqis from across the country will strengthen scholarship, provided institutions receive lasting support rather than promises attached to political prestige.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_security_compact: Political partnership is fragile when armed organizations answer to incompatible authorities. An agreed security compact will clarify integration and civilian command, with personnel obligations that must be honored if former rival forces are to work within the same order.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_trade_routes: Trade through the mountain districts depends on routes that are often difficult to maintain. Better infrastructure around Sulaymaniyah will connect local producers to a wider economy and make regional development less dependent on the reach of a few principal roads.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_student_exchange: A shared republic needs people who have studied and worked beyond the boundaries of their own community. Exchanges between Iraqi institutions will broaden students' experience and professional ties, while requiring places, travel support and continued cooperation from the education service.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_payroll: Overlapping security obligations make it difficult to know which forces the public is paying to maintain. Better records and inspections will reduce duplication, provided a professional administrative service can examine claims that influential commanders would rather keep beyond scrutiny.
COLDWAR_IRQ_puk_federal_mandate: A PUK-led government must earn confidence as a national administration as well as a Kurdish movement. Reviewing its federal programme will affirm the responsibilities it has accepted, while recognizing that constitutional partners possess a voice the governing party cannot simply disregard.
